This model asks whether children differ from one another not only in how many words they understand but in how much of that comprehension they turn into speech. It extends VG08 by adding a child-level random intercept to the production ratio as well as to the understood trajectory.

::: {.callout-important title="A development step — do not quote these numbers"}

VG09 exists to complete a structural argument, not to supply an estimate. The model of record for the Down syndrome understood-and-spoken estimands is **VG20**, which takes VG10's structure — VG09's, plus a per-draw Gaussian process anchor for stability — and adds a correlation between the child's two random intercepts; VG09 was once the recommended model and has since been superseded twice over.

That is a statement about model structure, not about how this fit sampled — the diagnostics section below is explicit that the fit reaching this page is a clean one. It nevertheless matters that the caution be taken seriously: VG09 and its predecessor VG08 differ in two ways at once — this model adds a child effect on the production ratio **and** migrates both dispersion blocks from the legacy constrained form to the two-anchor form — and they disagree substantially about how much of a child's comprehension is spoken at older ages, and about whether the gap between understanding and speaking stays open or closes. A reader who quotes either report is quoting a superseded number, and the two reports do not agree on what it should be.

:::

## Statistical model

Two outcomes are modelled together. Words understood is a bounded count out of the reference inventory with a Beta-Binomial likelihood. Words spoken is modelled _through_ comprehension rather than beside it: where a row carries a usable understood count, spoken words are drawn conditionally on it, $S \mid U \sim \operatorname{BetaBinomial}(U, q, \kappa_S)$, so $q$ is the fraction of the words a child understands that the same child also says. Rows without a usable understood count fall back to a marginal likelihood against the full reference inventory, and the same dispersion parameter governs both branches on two different denominators.

On the logit scale, comprehension and the production ratio each follow a straight-line developmental trend plus a Gaussian process term that lets the curve bend away from the line by as much as the data support:

$$f_U(a, s, i) = \text{intercept}_U + \text{slope}_U \cdot a_z + g_U(a) + \delta_U[s] + \delta^{\text{subj}}_U[i]$$
$$h(a, s, i) = \text{intercept}_q + \text{slope}_q \cdot a_z + g_q(a) + \delta_q[s] + \delta^{\text{subj}}_q[i]$$

Reading the symbols: $a$ is age and $a_z$ is age standardised to mean zero and unit standard deviation across the fitted frame; $s$ indexes the contributing study and $i$ the individual child; $g_U$ and $g_q$ are the Gaussian process terms, so "intercept plus slope" is the trend and $g$ is the wiggle around it. $f_U$ is the logit of the expected proportion understood, $p_U = \operatorname{sigmoid}(f_U)$, and $h$ is the logit of the production ratio, $q = \operatorname{sigmoid}(h)$. Expected spoken proportion is the product, $p_S = p_U \cdot q$.

Neither trend line is given a prior directly. Priors are placed instead on the expected proportion at two reference ages — an opinion about vocabulary at an age is something a reader can hold, an intercept at age zero is not. One caution on reading them: the anchors parameterise the straight-line component only. The fitted trajectory at a reference age is the anchor plus whatever the Gaussian process adds there, and in this model the process is unconstrained at the anchors — so they are coordinates of the trend, not exact values of the fitted curve at those ages.

### The two levels of grouping

Both random intercepts are written in **non-centred** form, $\delta = \tau z$, which describes the same distribution as drawing $\delta$ directly at scale $\tau$ but is far easier for the sampler to explore when $\tau$ is small.

- **Study effects** $\delta_U[s]$ and $\delta_q[s]$ use a **sum-to-zero** normal: the study offsets are constrained to add to zero across studies, and are therefore mildly negatively correlated with one another rather than independent. The constraint is what makes the population curve the _average study_ rather than an arbitrary reference study, and it is why the fitted study offsets can be read as deviations from that average.
- **Child effects** are now fitted on **both** outcomes: $\delta^{\text{subj}}_U[i] = \tau^{\text{subj}}_U z^U_i$ on comprehension and $\delta^{\text{subj}}_q[i] = \tau^{\text{subj}}_q z^q_i$ on the production ratio, each with a standard normal deviate. The second of these is the whole point of the model, and the parameter $\tau^{\text{subj}}_q$ is the one quantity VG09 exists to add.

The motivation is symmetry. If differences between children justify a child effect on how many words they understand, the same logic applies to how much of that comprehension they say: some children are talkers and some are not, and that is a persistent property of the child rather than noise in one administration. With both effects in place, the residual dispersion on each outcome should describe variability _within_ an occasion rather than persistent differences between children.

One consequence of adding a child effect on $q$ deserves stating before any figure is read. A curve drawn with all random effects set to zero is not the average of children's curves, because the logit link is nonlinear; adding a child effect on the production ratio therefore changes what the zero-effect curve means, and this model's population $q$ curve is not directly comparable with VG08's even though both are labelled the same way. It also means that, unlike in VG08, the median unseen child in this model does not speak the same number of words as the population curve implies. Both facts are properties of the structure, not signs of instability.

### Two different predictions, and which figure shows which

::: {.callout-important title="Population-level or subject-marginal?"}

The same age curve can be drawn two ways, and they differ by roughly an order of magnitude in width. Every figure caption below states which one it is.

- **Population-level** sets every random effect to zero: a conditional zero-effect trajectory — approximately the **median** child in the average study, not the average of children's curves, because the inverse-logit link is nonlinear (the consequence spelled out above). Its interval carries uncertainty about that reference trajectory only. This is what the production ratio, the comprehension–production gap, the expected-count curves, the age derivatives and the dispersion curves show, and it is what the `p_population_*` and `Ey_population_*` columns of the summary tables report. The unprefixed historical `p_*` and `Ey_*` columns carry the same population-level meaning.
- **Subject-marginal** draws a fresh child's random effects — on comprehension _and_ on the production ratio — for every posterior draw, and keeps that one child across the whole age grid. It answers _where would one more, unseen child fall?_ and is much wider. This is what the joint trajectory figures, the predictive ratio and predictive scatter, and every posterior predictive count artefact (PMF, CDF, count distributions, median trends) show, and it is what the `Y_*`, `P(Y<=k)`, `p_subject_marginal_*` and `Ey_subject_marginal_*` columns report.

Confusing the two is the single easiest way to misread this report: the population band answers a question about a group average, and only the subject-marginal band answers a question about a child.

:::

## Priors {#sec-priors}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
from vocab_growth.report_cells import render_priors_table

render_priors_table()
```

The low-age anchors encode a floor expectation on both outcomes: few words understood, and a small fraction of them spoken, at the younger reference age. The high-age anchors are deliberately broad, so the prior rules out neither a low nor a high later vocabulary before the data are seen. The production-ratio anchors are not merely broad regularisation — the high one was recalibrated against directly observed spoken and understood pairs and carries real information about the conversion rate, which makes it a named sensitivity target in `docs/models/PRIORS.md`. The GP length-scale and amplitude priors permit smooth departures from the anchor-defined trend and no more.

Three random-effect scales appear in the table above, and the last of them, the between-child scale on the production ratio, is the parameter this model adds to VG08. Judge each on the odds reading the table gives: a scale of one logit means a child one standard deviation above average has roughly $e$ times the odds of saying any given word they understand. The child-level priors are the wider of the two levels, because children within a study were expected to differ more than studies differ from each other, and because a subject scale set too tight would force the residual dispersion to keep absorbing between-child variation — the very thing the effect was added to stop. The scale used here replaces a substantially tighter earlier one that every subject-scale parameter in the model family sat in conflict with.

### Dispersion

Both dispersion blocks use the **two-anchor** form, with priors stated as $\kappa$ at two reference ages rather than as an intercept at the pool's mean age plus a slope. Two things follow. The prior is then directly comparable with a per-age dispersion estimate and does not shift meaning if the pool's age distribution changes. And, unlike the parameterisation VG08 retains, this form places no constrained slope prior on the age trend at all — the legacy form's failure mode, in which the Down syndrome joint fits put the slope magnitude about four standard deviations into the tail of its half-normal prior with negative contraction (a prior-scale conflict, not a boundary pin), cannot arise here, and a rising $\kappa$ is representable as well as a falling one. Because this migration arrives together with the new `q` child effect, dispersion comparisons between VG08 and VG09 mix the two changes.

These prior medians are **conditional** estimates. This model carries study and child random intercepts on both outcomes, so its $\kappa$ describes what is left once a child's own level is known, not the total spread between children at an age. A dispersion prior calibrated marginally would be badly wrong here, and that substitution is a large error rather than a rounding one.

The Down syndrome joint frame is the thinnest the calibration covers, and there is no larger pool to draw on, since every Down syndrome model loads the same unfiltered records. On it the estimator recovers a known $\kappa$ with a one-directional downward bias that grows with the level, so its estimates are lower bounds. The medians used here are the **uncorrected** calibration: an earlier a-priori bias correction — each estimate divided by the bias measured at its level — was dropped at the 2026-08-19 recalibration, noticed only after the promotion, and kept dropped as a stated position (the measured consequence is under 1% on reported $\kappa$ below 48 months; see `notes/202608191800-kappa-components-not-estimands.md` §9). The prior widths are the widest anywhere in the model family in consequence. What is not in doubt is that the previous prior was wrong: its half-normal slope prior was far too narrow for the fitted concentration trend, leaving the posterior in its extreme tail with negative contraction. See `docs/models/PRIORS.md`.

## Prior predictive checks {#sec-prior-predictive}

These simulate trajectories from the priors alone, before the data are seen. One scope limit must be read first: the figures below are **population mean functions** — they set the study and child effects to zero and draw no Beta-Binomial counts, so no between-study, between-child or count-level variation appears in them, and they cannot validate the random-effect scales, the dispersion priors, or the plausibility of simulated child spread — even though this model now carries two child effects whose priors deserve that check. Read them as a plausibility test on the mean structure, with three criteria: young children should usually sit near the floor on both outcomes; older trajectories should not be forced towards the ceiling; and the production ratio should be free to rise across development without being pinned near zero or near one. A prior that fails any of these would be shaping the answer rather than permitting it.

## Data {#sec-frame}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
from vocab_growth.report_cells import render_frame_composition

render_frame_composition()
```

The fitted frame pools administrations from several international studies of children with Down syndrome onto the common reference inventory. Its size, the number of rows carrying each outcome, and the modelled age range are in the _Model at a glance_ block above, read from this fit's own manifest.

Two features of the pool shape everything below. Comprehension is recorded on fewer administrations than production, so the understood curve rests on less data than the spoken one at every age. And the pool is weighted towards younger children with small spoken vocabularies, which is why the lower edge of the spoken predictive band sits near zero for a long stretch of the age range: at those ages a child saying almost nothing is an ordinary observation, not an outlier. Several classes of defective record — partial administrations, duplicated outcome columns, implausible production signatures, and children recorded only at their form's ceiling — are masked by default; the project's data documentation records each and the flag that reinstates it for sensitivity analysis.

```{python}
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import pandas as pd

descriptive_stats = pd.read_csv("descriptive_statistics.csv", index_col=0)
descriptive_stats
```

::: {.callout-note}

The normality tests in this table are reported for completeness. They are not a check on the model: both outcomes are bounded counts, which are not expected to be normally distributed, and the model does not assume that they are. Note also that the two outcomes are not observed on the same rows — the glance block above gives the count for each — so the understood and spoken columns are not summaries of one common set of children.

:::

The table above reports, for each parameter, whether the chains agree with one another (R-hat) and how many independent samples the correlated draws are worth (ESS). This project requires R-hat no greater than 1.01 and ESS of at least 400 for **every** parameter — including the random-effect elements, which the table itself does not list — before a fit may be reported at all, so a fit that reaches this page has already cleared those thresholds, or carries a recorded exception disclosed above. Any soft-tier mark (divergent transitions, or a low energy BFMI) would appear as a warning immediately above the table; where no warning appears, there was none to declare.

::: {.callout-note title="What to watch in this model"}

@fig-pair is capped at the number of panels that stay legible, so it shows only the first few parameters: the two understood anchors, the understood GP length-scale and amplitude, and the two production-ratio anchors. That subset is well chosen for the trade-off it can reveal — a diagonal ridge between an anchor and the GP amplitude would mean the data cannot say whether the curve's level comes from the straight line or from the bend. The random-effect scales and the dispersion parameters are **not** in this figure; read them from the diagnostics table and @fig-trace instead.

For @fig-posterior, compare each marginal with its prior figure earlier in this report. A parameter whose posterior is indistinguishable from its prior has not been informed by the data, and any conclusion resting on it is a restatement of the prior.

:::

::: {.callout-note title="A note on this model's history"}

Earlier VG09 fits genuinely did sample badly. Adding a second child effect gave the model several ways to explain the same level and the same heterogeneity — the production-ratio intercept, its Gaussian process, the study effects, the child effects and the spoken dispersion can all compete — and the resulting posterior had a ridge that longer tuning did not remove. That history is real, it is recorded in the project's sampler-diagnostics notes, and it is why VG10 was built.

Two registered changes since removed it: the Gaussian process amplitude prior on the production ratio was widened, having earlier been tightened on a mis-scoped rationale, and this model's dispersion block was migrated to the two-anchor form, removing the narrow constrained slope prior whose extreme tail the legacy posterior had been pushed into. Both are visible in the priors table above, and the fit reported on this page is the result.

The conclusion to draw is narrow. **VG09 remains a development step because the model of record adds structure this model lacks, not because VG09 samples badly** — on the evidence above it does not. Read the diagnostics table for what this fit did, and read this note as history.

:::

### How much do children and studies differ?

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
from vocab_growth.report_cells import render_variation_table

render_variation_table()
```

This is the table VG09 was built to produce, and it is the first in the lineage to carry all four rows. Compare the two child rows with the two study rows: they say how much of the modelled variation in each outcome is between children within a study, and how much is between the studies themselves. Then compare the two child rows with each other — the production ratio is the one that answers whether children differ more in what they understand or in how much of it they say.

A large child-level scale is not a defect. It is the finding that children of the same age with Down syndrome differ widely from one another, which is why a population average is a poor description of any individual, and why the subject-marginal bands elsewhere in this report are so much wider than the population ones.

Read this table together with the dispersion figures below rather than instead of them. Once a child's own level on an outcome is absorbed by its random intercept, the remaining $\kappa$ describes what is left _given_ that level — residual, occasion-level variability — and it must not be read as "how much children differ at this age". That quantity is in this table, not in $\kappa$. In principle the two effects can be seen working by comparing each dispersion curve with the same curve in VG07, which has neither child effect, and in VG08, which has only the comprehension one — but that comparison is confounded here: VG09's dispersion blocks are also on a different parameterisation from VG07's and VG08's, so cross-model differences in $\kappa$ mix the effect of the new hierarchy with the effect of the prior change.

## Posterior predictions {#sec-predictions}

### Joint trajectory

![Predicted vocabulary for an unseen child: **subject-marginal**, with a fresh child's random effects drawn for each posterior draw and held across the whole age grid. Points are the observed administrations.](joint_trajectory.png){#fig-joint-trajectory .lightbox fig-align="left"}

![The same **subject-marginal** prediction with the 50% inner and 89% outer equal-tailed intervals drawn explicitly.](joint_trajectory_intervals.png){#fig-joint-trajectory-intervals .lightbox fig-align="left"}

These are the widest bands in the report, and correctly so: they describe where a single unseen child might fall, not where the group average lies. Because this model carries a child effect on the production ratio as well as on comprehension, the spoken band here is wider relative to its population curve than VG08's is, and its median sits below the population median rather than on top of it. The comprehension curve stops earlier than the production curve because the two outcomes carry different reporting caps, which the _Model at a glance_ block states; the evidence for comprehension thins out earlier, so the model declines to publish an understood curve past that point.

### Production ratio

The production ratio $q(a)$ is the fraction of the words a child understands at age $a$ that the same child also says. It is what separates _knowing more words_ from _saying more of the words you know_.

![The **population-level** production ratio against age: the conditional zero-effect trajectory — approximately the median child in the average study — and not the average of children's own ratios.](production_rate.png){#fig-production-rate .lightbox fig-align="left"}

![The same **population-level** ratio, plotted against expected words understood rather than against age.](production_rate_by_understood.png){#fig-production-rate-by-understood .lightbox fig-align="left"}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
from vocab_growth.report_cells import render_conditional_production_check

render_conditional_production_check()
```


@fig-production-rate-by-understood re-plots the identical quantity with comprehension on the horizontal axis. It answers a different question from the age plot: not _how old is this child?_ but _how far along in comprehension is this child?_ — which is the more useful framing when children of the same age are at very different stages. The horizontal axis is age re-expressed as comprehension, so it stretches where vocabulary grows fast and compresses where it does not; it is not an independent variable the model conditions on.

![The ratio of **subject-marginal** predicted spoken to predicted understood counts.](production_rate_predictive.png){#fig-production-rate-predictive .lightbox fig-align="left"}

@fig-production-rate-predictive is a different quantity from the two above and the difference is easy to miss. $q(a)$ is a ratio of expectations — one smooth curve divided by another. The predictive figure is a distribution of ratios of _drawn counts_ for a single simulated child, and the spoken count is drawn from a distribution whose denominator is itself a drawn understood count. At young ages that makes it far more variable than $q(a)$, and gives it a floor at zero that the smooth ratio does not have. Read it as "what ratio might one child show", not as an estimate of $q$.

Above the high age anchor, $q$'s mean is held level by the mean clamp rather than allowed to extrapolate. The Gaussian process term is still free to move there, so the curve is not flat at the oldest ages, but it is not being carried upward by a straight line running past the last age the prior speaks to either.

### Comprehension-production gap

![The **population-level** difference between expected words understood and expected words spoken.](comprehension_production_gap.png){#fig-gap .lightbox fig-align="left"}

The gap is the number of words the reference child — every random effect at zero, approximately the median child — understands but does not yet say. It widens while comprehension outpaces production and narrows again once the production ratio catches up, so it has a peak at an intermediate age; the headline table above gives the peak and where it falls. Whether the gap then closes or stays open is a substantive claim about development, and it is one of the quantities on which this model and VG08 disagree — a further reason to take neither as final.

### Words understood versus words spoken

![Expected words spoken against expected words understood, **population-level**, one curve per posterior draw.](understood_vs_spoken.png){#fig-understood-vs-spoken .lightbox fig-align="left"}

![The same relationship in **subject-marginal** predicted counts, one curve per posterior draw for a freshly drawn child.](understood_vs_spoken_predictive.png){#fig-understood-vs-spoken-predictive .lightbox fig-align="left"}

The pair differ in estimand, not just in scatter. The first shows what the model believes about the _average_ relationship between comprehension and production, and its spread is uncertainty about that average. The second shows the counts an individual child might actually record, and its spread additionally carries between-child differences — on both outcomes in this model — and the noise in a single administration.

### Receptive to expressive vocabulary {#sec-spoken-given-understood}

**How are comprehension and production related, cross-sectionally?** The joint model links them structurally through the production ratio: the expected number of words a child _says_ is the number they _understand_ scaled by $q(a)$,

$$\mathbb{E}[\,\text{spoken} \mid \text{understood} = N,\ \text{age} = a\,] \approx N \cdot q(a).$$

Read across from a child's comprehension score to the line for their age, and the vertical position is the number of words the model expects them to say. This is the same information as the production-ratio figure above, expressed in the units a practitioner actually works in. Two cautions attach to it. First, $q(a)$ is a cross-sectional conversion proportion, not a mechanism: the figure is **not** evidence that raising a particular child's receptive vocabulary would cause a matching expressive gain. Second, the slopes are the _population_ production ratio — the zero-effect reference child's conversion rate, not this child's. The between-child scale for $q$ in the variation table above is precisely the amount by which an individual child may sit off these lines, and it is not small, so the shaded band around each line is far narrower than the range of children.

## Posterior predictions -- words understood

### Posterior summary table

$p$ is the latent success probability — the underlying proportion of the reference inventory a child is expected to understand at a given age. $Ey$ is the expected count implied by $p$, and reflects uncertainty in the mean trajectory alone. $Y$ is a draw from the posterior predictive distribution, and reflects both that uncertainty **and** between-child and occasion-level variability, so it is much the wider of the two. The `_population_` and `_subject_marginal_` columns state the two estimands explicitly; the unprefixed columns are the population-level ones. Quote $Y$ or a `subject_marginal` column when asking where a single child might fall, and a `population` column when asking about the group average. Columns labelled `ci` are the 89% outer interval and those labelled `ci50` the 50% inner interval, both equal-tailed.

### Dispersion $\kappa$ -- understood


![How the dispersion parameter for words understood changes with age, with uncertainty intervals. **Population-level**.](posterior_kappa_u.png){#fig-kappa-u .lightbox fig-align="left"}

Lower $\kappa$ means **greater** residual variability relative to the mean; higher $\kappa$ means less. The direction is easy to misread, so the headline table above restates it as a variance inflation factor, where a larger number means a wider spread. Because this model carries a child random intercept on understood, this $\kappa$ is what remains once a child's own level is known.

## Posterior predictions -- words spoken

### Posterior summary table

The columns mean the same as in the understood table above, with two differences worth knowing. This table runs to a later age, because production is reported past the comprehension cap, and its last rows sit above the high age anchor, where the production ratio is held level by the mean clamp; what still moves there is the comprehension trend, so those rows are a levelled-off projection rather than an estimate the data support. And the predictive draws behind $Y$ are nested: for the paired records each spoken count is drawn out of a _drawn_ understood count, not out of the full reference inventory.

## Expected vocabulary by month {#sec-monthly}

A finer companion to the tables above: one row per whole month. Each figure draws **both** estimands, which is what makes it the clearest single answer to the population-versus-individual question — the filled band is the expected count with parameter uncertainty only (population-level), and the dashed outline is the range a single child might fall in (subject-marginal). The difference in width between them is the difference between a statement about a group and a statement about a child.

The `n_obs` column in the tables gives the number of observations near each age, which is the honest guide to where these expectations rest on data and where they rest on the model.

## Limits {#sec-limits}

- **A development step, not a source of numbers.** VG20 is the model of record for these estimands, and the lineage between here and there adds a Gaussian process anchor and a correlation between the child's two random intercepts, neither of which this model has. Nothing in this report should be quoted as a finding about vocabulary in Down syndrome — and the point is not academic, since VG09 and VG08 disagree materially about the production ratio at older ages.
- **The population curves are not averages of children.** With a child effect on the production ratio and a nonlinear link, the zero-effect curve is a particular child-level trajectory rather than the mean of the cohort's, and it is not comparable with the identically-labelled curve in a model without that effect.
- **Child effects are constant offsets.** Every child's latent trajectory is parallel to every other's on both outcomes: relative standing is fixed at every age, rank changes are impossible, and developmental tracking is therefore perfect by construction rather than estimated. Do not read age variation in $\kappa$ as changing between-child spread once the child effects are in place.
- **The two child effects are forced independent, and for some children only their product is identified.** Children contributing spoken observations but no understood observation at any wave — over 150 children in the current frame — chiefly inform the product of their two effects, so the individual split for them is driven by the hierarchy and the priors. The recorded fits also contradict the independence assumption itself: VG10's fitted deviations correlate positively, and VG20 estimates the correlation directly. Use VG20 for child-level inference.
- **Above the high age anchor the production ratio is clamped**, and the reported comprehension range stops before the spoken range does. Both are stated in the _Model at a glance_ block. Rows beyond those points are carried by the model's smoothness assumptions rather than by observations; the monthly tables' `n_obs` column shows where that begins.
- **The dispersion priors are lower bounds.** The calibration for this frame recovers a known $\kappa$ with a one-directional downward bias; the prior medians use the uncorrected calibration — the earlier a-priori correction was dropped, as a stated position — and the priors are correspondingly wide.
- **Age is not a mechanism.** Everything reported is an association with age, not an effect of it, and the receptive-to-expressive mapping is a cross-sectional conversion, not a causal claim.
- **The reference inventory is a harmonisation.** Counts from different checklists are placed on a common scale; it is a unit of measurement, not an instrument any child sat.
- **Not every spoken record is modelled as nested.** Records lacking a usable understood count, and records whose reported spoken count exceeds the reported understood count, use the marginal fallback described under Statistical model, and are informed by the production ratio less directly than the paired records are.
